mustKnow: V = I × R (volts, amps, ohms), and its rearrangements R = V ÷ I and I = V ÷ R

Ohm's law: current directly proportional to voltage for a metal wire at constant temperature

notOnThisSpec: Diodes, thermistors and LDRs and their graphs
Potential difference as the required word (CCEA says voltage)

mustBeAbleTo: Recall and use V = I × R in all three arrangements, with voltage in volts, current in amps and resistance in ohms
Convert milliamps to amps before substituting, and amps to milliamps when the answer asks for mA
Draw the P6 circuit: ammeter and variable resistor in series with the wire, voltmeter in parallel across it
Explain how the wire is kept at constant temperature: small currents, switch off between readings
Name the independent, dependent and control variables in P6
Spot an anomalous reading in a P6 table by its V ÷ I, and repeat it or leave it out of the line of best fit
Plot voltage (y-axis) against current (x-axis) and draw a line or curve of best fit
State Ohm's law and say how a straight line through the origin shows it
Find a resistance from the gradient of the P6 graph and give its unit, the ohm
Higher: show that a filament lamp's resistance increases by working out V ÷ I at different currents
Higher: explain the lamp's curve through temperature, vibrating atoms and electron collisions
sheet.howExamined: P2, 1 hour 15 minutes, 70 marks at Foundation and 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. V = IR comes as a three- or four-mark calculation (equation, substitution with any milliamps converted, answer); the filament lamp is a Higher question with symbols to insert in a practical circuit, a graph to complete with a label and a unit, and a five-mark explanation of the curve. Unit 7 Booklet A has set P6 itself (readings, the temperature precaution, the variables, the graph, its gradient and unit); Booklet B asks for meter positions, a plotted graph, R = V/I and the trend.
traps: Putting the voltmeter anywhere but across the component, or a fixed resistor in the variable resistor's gap; describing the curve only as the current rising and never mentioning the resistance (Summer 2023 U7 Physics Booklet B Q4, Higher)
Drawing a switch or a plain resistor where the variable resistor goes, and explaining the lamp's curve by brightness instead of temperature and collisions (Summer 2025 P2 Higher Q9)
Leaving 600 mA as 600 in V = IR instead of converting it to 0.6 A (Summer 2023 P2 Higher Q6)
Missing the milliamp conversion again in an Ohm's law calculation (Summer 2025 P2 Higher Q3)
Placing the voltmeter in series in the lamp circuit, and using a non-linear scale on the graph (Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q3, Higher)
Giving voltage as the independent variable, and leaving out controlled variables such as the wire's material, length and thickness (Summer 2023 U7 Physics Booklet A Q1, Higher)

Working out current ÷ voltage on the calculator instead of voltage ÷ current, and not seeing that V ÷ I is the resistance in ohms; writing positive correlation instead of directly proportional (Summer 2023 U7 Physics Booklet A Q1, Foundation)
Starting from an incorrect variant of R = V/I, which scores nothing even if the number comes out right (Summer 2024 P2 Foundation Q7)
Starting from a wrong equation in the resistance calculation at Higher too (Summer 2024 P2 Higher Q4)
Placing the voltmeter in series instead of across the wire, and missing the directly proportional relationship (Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q2, Foundation)

workedExamples.stem:
A filament lamp has 0.6 V across it when the current is 0.10 A, and 3.6 V across it when the current is 0.30 A.
Show that the lamp's resistance increases as the current increases. [3]

steps.working: R = V ÷ I at each current, using the voltage and the current from the same reading.
steps.decision: The spec asks you to show the change by taking the ratio of voltage to current at different currents.

options: Because the lamp's resistance is different at each current, so each reading needs its own ratio
Because the curve's gradient is the resistance
Because Ohm's law holds for a lamp as well as a wire
whyMenu.explain: A lamp's graph is a curve, so no single gradient means resistance. The ratio V ÷ I at each reading gives the resistance at that current, and comparing the ratios shows the change.

steps.decision: First ratio.
Second ratio, at the larger current.

steps.working: 12 Ω is more than 6 Ω, so the resistance increases as the current increases.
steps.decision: Finish with the comparison in words: the question asked you to show the increase, so say it.

options.feedback: Right: the larger current gives the larger ratio.
The two ratios are different, so the resistance has changed.
The ratio at the larger current is the bigger one, so the resistance has gone up.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: 6 Ω at 0.10 A and 12 Ω at 0.30 A: the resistance increases.

steps.working: Choose two points far apart on the line: the origin (0, 0) and (0.35 A, 2.8 V).
steps.decision: Points on the line, as far apart as possible, make the division least sensitive to small reading errors.

options: Because far-apart points on the line give the most accurate gradient
Because the table values are always wrong
Because the gradient must start at zero
whyMenu.explain: A big triangle spreads any reading error over a big rise and run. Use the line, not two close table values.

steps.decision: Rise is the change up the side (voltage); run is the change across (current).
A gradient's unit is the unit up the side divided by the unit across. Volts per amp is the ohm, because this gradient is the resistance.

options.feedback: Right: volts per amp is the ohm.
That divides the wrong way. The gradient is volts per amp.
The gradient is a ratio of two quantities, so its unit is a ratio too: volts per amp.

workedExamples.stem:
A 9 V supply is connected across a 450 Ω resistor.
Calculate the current in the resistor. Give your answer in mA. [3]

steps.decision: The current is the unknown, so rearrange V = I × R to leave I on its own.

options: Because I is the unknown, and dividing both sides of V = I × R by R leaves I alone
Because a current is always the voltage times the resistance
Because the answer is wanted in milliamps
whyMenu.explain: Start from the equation you know and rearrange for the unknown. Multiplying would give volts times ohms, which is not a current.

steps.decision: Work in amps first: volts divided by ohms gives amps.
The question asks for milliamps, so multiply by 1000. Stopping at the amps would give a number in the wrong unit.

workedExamples.stem:
A student's P6 readings for a metal wire: 0.20 A with 1.5 V, 0.40 A with 3.0 V, 0.60 A with 4.5 V.
Show that the wire obeys Ohm's law over these readings, and give its resistance. [4]

steps.decision: Work out V ÷ I for each reading. If the wire obeys Ohm's law, every ratio comes out the same.

options: Because a constant V ÷ I means the voltage and the current rise in the same proportion
Because Ohm's law says the voltage is always bigger than the current
Because dividing makes the numbers smaller and easier to compare
whyMenu.explain: Directly proportional means one quantity is always the same multiple of the other, which is a constant V ÷ I. On a graph it is a straight line through the origin.

steps.decision: The second reading, the same way.
The third reading. All three ratios can now be compared.

steps.working: Every ratio is 7.5 Ω, so the current is directly proportional to the voltage: the wire obeys Ohm's law, and its resistance is 7.5 Ω.
steps.decision: Finish in words: name the constant ratio and say what it shows.

options.text: the ratios are all the same, so the current is directly proportional to the voltage
options.feedback: Right: a constant V ÷ I is what directly proportional means.

options.text: the voltages and currents both rise, so the wire obeys Ohm's law
options.feedback: Rising together is a trend, which a lamp shows too. The law needs the ratio to stay the same.

options.text: the ratios differ, so the wire does not obey Ohm's law
options.feedback: Each ratio comes to 7.5 Ω; they are the same.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: V ÷ I = 7.5 Ω for every reading: directly proportional, so the wire obeys Ohm's law; R = 7.5 Ω.

twin.stem: Readings for another wire: 0.25 A with 1.0 V, 0.50 A with 2.0 V, 0.75 A with 3.0 V. V ÷ I is the same for each. What is the wire's resistance? [2]

workedExamples.stem:
A filament lamp has 2.0 V across it when the current is 0.25 A, and 6.0 V across it when the current is 0.50 A.
Calculate how much its resistance increases between these two currents. [3]

steps.decision: A lamp's resistance is different at every current, so take V ÷ I at each reading, with both values from that reading.

options: Because the lamp's resistance changes with current, so each reading needs its own V ÷ I
Because the gradient between the two readings is the resistance
Because the two currents should be added first
whyMenu.explain: On a curve the gradient between two readings is not V ÷ I at either: here it would give 16 Ω, which is neither resistance. Divide each voltage by its own current.

steps.decision: The same method at the larger current.
The question asks how much it increases, so subtract the smaller resistance from the larger.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: 8 Ω rising to 12 Ω: an increase of 4 Ω.

items.stem: Before we start: what is the unit of electric current?

options.feedback: The amp. Current is measured with an ammeter, in amps.
The volt is the unit of voltage. Current is measured in amps.
The watt is the unit of power. Current is measured in amps.

items.stem: Before we start: how is an ammeter connected to measure the current through a lamp?

options.feedback: In series, so the lamp's current passes through it.
That is how a voltmeter is connected. An ammeter goes in series.

options.text: either way, it makes no difference
options.feedback: It matters: only in series does the lamp's current pass through the ammeter.

items.stem: Before we start: if a = b × c, which of these is correct?

options.feedback: Right. Divide both sides by c.
To undo × c you divide by c: b = a ÷ c.
That is upside down. Divide a by c: b = a ÷ c.

items.stem: Before we start: how many amps is 500 mA?

options.feedback: 0.5 A. Milli means a thousandth, so divide by 1000.
Milli means a thousandth: divide by 1000, not 10. 500 mA = 0.5 A.
Milliamps are smaller than amps, so the number of amps is smaller: divide by 1000.

items.stem: Which equation gives the resistance of a component?

options.feedback: Right: volts for each amp.
That is upside down. Resistance is the voltage divided by the current.
Multiplying voltage by current gives something else entirely. Resistance is V ÷ I.

items.stem: A current of 400 mA flows through a 20 Ω resistor. What is the voltage across it?

options.feedback: Right: 0.4 A × 20 Ω.
The current went in as milliamps. Convert first: 400 mA = 0.4 A.
That divides the current by the resistance. V = I × R multiplies them.

items.stem: In P6, what does the graph of voltage against current look like for a metal wire at constant temperature?

options.text: a straight line through the origin
options.feedback: Right. Straight and through the origin means proportional.

options.text: a straight line that starts above the origin
options.feedback: A line that does not pass through the origin is not proportional. The wire's line goes through the origin.
That is the filament lamp. A metal wire at constant temperature gives a straight line through the origin.

items.stem: In P6 the student sets each current and then reads the voltage. Which is the independent variable?

options.feedback: Right: it is the one being set.
The voltage is measured after the current is set, so it is the dependent variable.
The temperature is kept constant: it is a control variable.

items.stem: Why does a filament lamp's resistance increase as the current through it increases?

options.text: the filament gets hotter, its atoms vibrate more and electrons collide with them more often
options.feedback: Right: temperature, vibration, collisions.

options.text: the lamp gets brighter, and the brighter light holds back the current
options.feedback: Brightness comes from the heat; it is not the cause. The resistance rises because the hotter atoms vibrate more and are hit more often.

options.text: the current is used up as it passes through the filament
options.feedback: Current is not used up. The resistance rises because a hotter filament's atoms vibrate more and electrons collide with them more often.

items.stem: In P6, where is the voltmeter connected?

options.feedback: Right: it compares the two ends of the wire.

options.text: in series, in the loop with the wire
options.feedback: In series it would read almost nothing useful. The voltmeter goes across the wire.

options.text: in series, next to the cell
options.feedback: A voltmeter never goes in the loop. It is connected across the wire it measures.

items.stem: A P6 graph has voltage in volts up the side and current in amps across. What is the unit of its gradient?

options.feedback: Right: the gradient is V ÷ I, the resistance.
That divides the wrong way. The gradient is the change up the side over the change across: V/A.
A gradient divides one quantity by another, so its unit is volts per amp, not volts times amps.

parts.stem:
The student needs to measure the current through the wire and the voltage across it, and to change the current to get a range of readings.
Name the component that goes in each gap. Choose each name from the list.
parts.workedSolution: (i) variable resistor, in the loop, to change the current. (ii) voltmeter, on the branch across the wire, so it compares the two ends of the wire. (iii) ammeter, in the loop, so the wire's current passes through it.

options.feedback: Right. A current heats the wire, and a hotter wire has a higher resistance.

options.text: so that the readings are more reliable
options.feedback: Reliability comes from repeating readings. Switching off between readings is about the wire's temperature.

options.text: so the ammeter can go back to zero
options.feedback: The meters do not need resetting. The switch is opened so the wire does not warm up.

scheme.for: to keep the temperature (of the wire) constant

parts.workedSolution: So the wire does not heat up: its temperature must stay constant for Ohm's law to apply.

hints: The student needs several different pairs of readings.
parts.stem: What is the variable resistor for?

options.text: to change the current, so a range of readings can be taken
options.feedback: Right. Each setting gives a new current and a new voltage.

options.text: to keep the current the same for every reading
options.feedback: It does the opposite: it changes the current so that several different readings can be taken.

options.text: to measure the resistance of the wire
options.feedback: Nothing in the circuit measures resistance directly: it is worked out from V ÷ I. The variable resistor changes the current.

scheme.for: to change (vary) the current / give a range of readings

parts.workedSolution: To change the current, so that a range of pairs of readings can be taken.

The temperature is kept the same: it is a control variable. The variable you set is the current.

parts.workedSolution: The current: it is the variable the student chooses and sets. The voltage is then measured, so it is the dependent variable.

hints: Use two points far apart on the line, not two close together.
Rise is the change in voltage; run is the change in current.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the run divided by the rise: current ÷ voltage. The gradient is the change up the side (voltage) divided by the change across (current).

parts.stem:
Use two points on the line to calculate its gradient.
Show your working out.

scheme.for: gradient = rise ÷ run (change in voltage ÷ change in current)
values from two points on the line, e.g. 2.5 ÷ 0.5

parts.workedSolution: Gradient = rise ÷ run. Using the origin and the point (0.5 A, 2.5 V): 2.5 ÷ 0.5 = 5.

hints: Divide the unit up the side by the unit across.

commonErrors.feedback: A gradient's unit is the unit up the side divided by the unit across: volts per amp, which is the ohm. Amps per volt is the division the wrong way round, and a single unit on its own misses the division.

parts.stem: State the unit of the gradient.
parts.workedSolution: Ω (ohms). The gradient is volts ÷ amps, which is the unit of resistance.

prompts.prompt: What shape is the P6 graph for a metal wire at constant temperature?
prompts.answer: A straight line through the origin.

prompts.prompt: In P6, how is the wire kept at a constant temperature?
prompts.answer: Use small currents and open the switch between readings.

prompts.prompt: On CCEA's P6 graph, which quantity goes up the side, and what does the gradient give?
prompts.answer: Voltage goes up the side, so the gradient (V ÷ I) is the resistance, in ohms.

prompts.prompt: How do you show from readings that a filament lamp's resistance increases?
prompts.answer: Work out R = V ÷ I at two or more different currents: the ratio is larger at the larger current.

prompts.prompt: Why does a filament lamp's resistance increase as the current increases?
prompts.answer: The filament's temperature rises, its atoms vibrate more, and the electrons collide with them more often.

prompts.prompt: In the P6 circuit, how are the ammeter, the voltmeter and the variable resistor connected?
prompts.answer: The ammeter and the variable resistor in series with the wire; the voltmeter in parallel across the wire.

findings.asked: Complete the circuit for a lamp's voltage-current graph, plot the graph, describe what it shows.
findings.wentWrong: Few got all three circuit marks: the voltmeter must go in parallel with the lamp and a variable resistor in the gap to give a range of readings; careless variable-resistor symbols lost the mark. Graphs were good apart from axis labels, poor scales by the least able, and ruler lines between points instead of a curve. Descriptions talked only of current rising with voltage and ignored the resistance.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Drew the voltmeter across the lamp, the variable resistor in series, a smooth curve, and said the resistance increases as the current rises.
findings.rule: The story of the graph is about resistance, not just current.

findings.asked: Circuit symbols, complete a filament-lamp characteristic, explain why it curves.
findings.wentWrong: Lamp, ammeter and voltmeter symbols were fine but a switch or a fixed resistor was drawn for the variable resistor; label, unit and origin marks were earned; only the most able understood the curve - even those who said the resistance rises could not say why, and the best answers linked it to temperature and more collisions.
findings.rule: The filament heats up, its ions vibrate more, electrons collide more often, resistance rises, so the current rises less for each extra volt.

findings.asked: Ohm's law calculation with a current given in milliamps.
findings.wentWrong: The method was fine but weaker candidates did not convert 600 mA to 0.6 A.
findings.rule: mA to A: divide by 1000 before substituting.

findings.asked: Electrical power over ten minutes, then an Ohm's law calculation in milliamps.
findings.wentWrong: The power formula was recalled but minutes were not converted to seconds; Ohm's law was known but the milliamp conversion was again missed by a significant minority.
findings.rule: Seconds and amps: convert first, then substitute.

findings.asked: Add a voltmeter to a circuit, plot the graph, calculate resistance, state how it changed.
findings.wentWrong: The symbol was known but the voltmeter was often placed in series; a few used a non-linear scale; R = V/I scored for those who recalled it; nearly all saw the resistance increasing.
findings.rule: Voltmeter in parallel across the component; a linear scale on each axis.

insight.ruleToRemember: V = I R with I in amps (divide mA by 1000). Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the component, variable resistor to change the current. A metal wire at constant temperature obeys Ohm's law (straight line through the origin); a filament lamp's graph curves because the filament gets hotter, electrons collide more often with the vibrating ions, and the resistance rises.
insight.aStarSignal: Explaining the curve with temperature, collisions and resistance in one causal chain, and drawing the practical circuit correctly without a scaffold.
